title: The command window and the command card
owns: app/renderer/command/**, app/main/commands/window.ts, app/main/commands/flow.ts (countdown), app/main/commands/visible-text.ts, the command window's creation in windows.ts (small hunk)

findings.title: Command window: Tab, Shift+Tab and Esc are swallowed by the terminal, so keyboard focus cannot leave it
findings.area: Command window: keyboard operability (WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap)
findings.scenario: A keyboard-only user presses Tab from a run's command block. Focus enters xterm's hidden 'Terminal input' textarea and stays there. Tab, Shift+Tab and Esc are all consumed: on an interactive run they are sent to the process as \t, ESC[Z and ESC. The Stop or Close button and the other tabs sit after the terminal in the DOM, so they are not reachable from inside it. Even a non-interactive run (typing hint: 'This command can't take typing here') traps focus the same way, because xterm cancels Tab before it checks disableStdin. The typing hint names no way out. Alt+Tab away and back lands on the terminal again. The only in-window recovery is a mouse click, or leaving the terminal via the tab strip (Shift+Tab wraps through BODY to Stop). The keyboard-only way to stop is the global Ctrl+Alt+X, which stops everything.
findings.evidence: Chromium run of dist/app/renderer/command with stubbed emberCommands (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/release-review/ux-a11y/xterm-trap.mjs and xterm-trap2.mjs). Tab order: tab button -> PRE.command -> TEXTAREA.xterm-helper-textarea and then it never moves. Five Tabs, one Shift+Tab and one Esc sent ['\t' x5, '\u001b[Z', '\u001b'] to the run (interactive case). In the non-interactive case nothing was sent and focus still did not move. DOM order in app/renderer/command/main.ts:278 is panel.append(header, block, host /*terminal*/, typing, foot /*status + Stop|Close*/). With term.attachCustomKeyEventHandler(e => e.key !== 'Tab') on xterm 5.5, Tab left the terminal (xterm-fix2.mjs). terminal.ts has no key handler.
findings.fix: In createRunTerminal call term.attachCustomKeyEventHandler. For non-interactive runs return false for Tab and Shift+Tab (or give the helper textarea tabindex=-1). For interactive runs keep Tab for the process but add a documented escape (for example Esc then Tab, or Ctrl+Shift+M as VS Code does) and name it in TYPING_HINT. Also move the status line and Stop|Close before the terminal in DOM and Tab order. Add a unit test next to renderer-command.test.ts.

findings.title: Keyboard trap in the terminal: Tab, Shift+Tab and Esc can't leave it, and Stop sits behind it
findings.scenario: A keyboard-only or screen-reader user tabs through a running tab: tab, command block, then the terminal's hidden textarea. Focus stays in the textarea for every further Tab, Shift+Tab and Esc (WCAG 2.1.2), and Stop/Close come after the terminal in DOM order (panel.append(header, block, host, typing, foot)). On Linux/macOS interactive runs each Tab is also sent to the program as \t: tabbing around while sudo's password prompt is waiting adds a tab character to the password. The terminal shows no focus indicator at all. Only Shift+Tab from a fresh window (wraps to Stop), the mouse or the stop chord escape.
findings.evidence: trap.mjs against the built page (xterm 5.5.0, real options): 'Tab trail: tab -> PRE.command -> TEXTAREA.xterm-helper-textarea -> TEXTAREA -> Shift+Tab=>TEXTAREA -> Escape=>TEXTAREA'. Interactive run: input messages [\t, ESC[Z, ESC, ESC[Z] were sent to the run. Non-interactive run: same trap, nothing sent. trap2.mjs: Shift+Tab from a fresh window lands on Stop. terminal.ts:32-36 only calls term.open(host); no tabIndex, no custom key handler, no :focus-within style on .term.
findings.fix: Put the footer (status + Stop/Close) before the terminal in DOM order or give it its own landmark. For non-interactive runs set term.textarea.tabIndex = -1. For interactive runs add term.attachCustomKeyEventHandler so Esc then Tab (or Ctrl+Shift+M) hands focus back, say so in the typing hint, and add .term:focus-within { box-shadow: var(--focus-ring) }.

findings.title: Command output is invisible to screen readers: xterm runs with screenReaderMode:false, so its rows are aria-hidden
findings.scenario: A blind user asks Ember to run 'npm test' or answers an interactive prompt such as sudo or ssh in the command window ('where you can watch and stop them'). A screen reader finds 'Terminal input' (an edit box) and nothing else: the program's output, prompts and errors are not in the accessibility tree. The user cannot read what the command printed, cannot read a prompt they are asked to type an answer to, and cannot tell why a run failed beyond the status line ('Ended with exit code 2'). This is the central surface of the new commands feature. The README and docs/COMMANDS-WSL-SSH.md do not list it among the limitations (L1-L26).
findings.evidence: CDP Accessibility.getFullAXTree for a run that received 'PASS src/a.test.ts / FAIL src/b.test.ts': the tabpanel contains only generic 'What the command shows' > textbox 'Terminal input'. No node contains 'PASS' or 'FAIL', and none is ignored-with-text. DOM: .xterm-rows has aria-hidden="true" and its text is 'PASS src/a.test.tsFAIL src/b.test.ts' (command2.mjs). In xterm 5.5, screenReaderMode:true adds .xterm-accessibility with an aria-live='assertive' region (xterm-fix.mjs); false adds nothing. The option is pinned at terminal-options.ts:43 ('exactly as §3.10 sets them'). A non-interactive run also still exposes a focusable 'Terminal input' textbox that accepts nothing, which is misleading.
findings.fix: Turn screenReaderMode on when assistive technology is active. Have main send sys.a11y.screenReaderOn() (it already exists) to the command page, or default to true, and pass it to terminalOptions. Update the options pin in renderer-command.test.ts. Give non-interactive runs a non-focusable helper textarea. Add the limitation to docs/COMMANDS-WSL-SSH.md if it stays.

findings.title: Announced commands start after a fixed 4 s with no keyboard hint; the Stop button is mouse-only and the countdown cannot be extended
findings.area: Timeouts and keyboard operability (WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable, 2.1.1)
findings.scenario: A user asks by voice or text for something Ember announces instead of asking about (a push, an overwrite they requested). The bubble says 'Pushing feature-x to origin, as you asked. On this computer. It starts in 4 seconds.' with a Stop button, and the command runs when the countdown ends. For a screen-reader, switch or slow-reading user that is too short to hear the announcement (about 20 words, 6 s or more at normal reading speed; the bubble's live region and Ember's own speech read it at the same time), find the control and act. The Stop button is in the overlay (focusable:false) or in the command window, which is opened with showInactive. Nothing in the bubble, the spoken text or the command window card says Ctrl+Alt+X stops it. Ordinary questions do carry a key hint, and announcements do not.
findings.evidence: flow.ts:175 `ANNOUNCE_MS = 4000`; flow.ts:700-710 awaits svc.window.announce(card, ANNOUNCE_MS). presenter.ts:634-646 announce() sets step: null, actions: [Stop] and calls onAnnounce(text), which speaks only the words. The questions' hint comes from Confirmer.keyHint (confirm.ts:222), which announcements do not use. renderer/command/main.ts:203-225 buildAnnounce has the countdown (role=timer, aria-live off by default) and Stop, with no key hint. commands/window.ts:228-230 reveal() uses showInactive. Live region content checked in overlay.mjs: 'Ember needs you: <title> <thought>', no key.
findings.fix: Lengthen the window when a screen reader is on (sys.a11y.screenReaderOn()) or add a 'More time to react' setting (for example 15 s or ask-always). Put 'Press Ctrl+Alt+X to stop' in the announcement bubble, in its live-region text and in the spoken line. Consider answering the announcement with Ctrl+Alt+N like a question.

findings.title: Typing an answer into a command: terminal isn't focused (keystrokes vanish) and Ctrl+V doesn't paste
findings.scenario: The user approves 'sudo apt install ...' (or ssh-keygen, git over https). The tab appears showing '[sudo] password for ana:'. They type at once: nothing is received, because keyboard focus is on <body>, and with echo off they can't tell. After clicking the terminal they paste from their password manager with Ctrl+V: xterm sends a literal ^V (0x16) instead of pasting, so the password is wrong and sudo burns an attempt. Ctrl+Shift+V and Shift+Insert do paste but nothing says so. This hits Windows users too, for WSL and SSH runs (interactive PTY).
findings.evidence: term-focus.mjs: after the state push and the prompt output, document.activeElement is BODY; page.keyboard.type('hunter2') produced no 'input' message. term-paste.mjs with the clipboard set: Control+v -> input '\u0016'; Control+Shift+v -> input 's3cret-passw0rd'; Shift+Insert -> pasted. grep: the only focus() call in renderer/command is the tab strip (main.ts:293); createRunTerminal never focuses.
findings.fix: Focus the terminal when an interactive run's tab is shown and the window is active (term.focus()). Add term.attachCustomKeyEventHandler returning false for Ctrl+V (let the browser paste into the textarea; don't call navigator.clipboard, main denies that permission) and for Ctrl+C when term.hasSelection(). Mention paste in the typing hint.

findings.title: A command that asks for a password: nothing tells the user, later runs never raise the window, and it times out silently after 2 minutes
findings.scenario: The worker prompt tells the model 'if a command asks for a password, the user types it in the command window'. After the first command the window stays open but is never raised again: reveal() only shows it when hidden or when a card/countdown is up. The user's browser sits on top; the model runs git clone https://github.com/acme/private; git prints "Username for 'https://github.com':" and waits. The bubble says 'Running a command', the window is buried, and at 120 s it ends 'Stopped after 2 min: it took too long.' The user was never told a prompt was waiting.
findings.evidence: raise.mjs with the real controller: first attach -> calls 'showInactive'; with the window now visible, a second attach plus output "Username for 'https://github.com': " -> calls only 'send:output' (no moveTop, no show, no cue). grep of app/main/commands, targets and renderer/command finds no 'waiting for you' signal; prompts.ts only withholds the answer from the model. The task card's only action is Stop (tasks.ts:295).
findings.fix: On every attach, raise the window without focus (setAlwaysOnTop pulse or moveTop). When an interactive run's output ends in a prompt (reuse SECRET_PROMPT, or no newline for ~2 s) flash the tab, put 'A command is waiting for you to type' in the task's bubble with a 'Show' button, and optionally notify. Reset the timeout clock while it waits for the user.

findings.title: Closing the command window leaves running commands running, unseen, with no way back except Settings
findings.area: command window: lifecycle, how to stop it
findings.scenario: A user watching a long command (npm install, a build, a copy) clicks the window's close button, as they would with a terminal, believing it stops. The window is destroyed, the command keeps running, and nothing says so. The task card only offers Stop for the whole task; Settings > Computers > 'Open the command window' is the only route back to the tab and its Stop. It also breaks the R1 promise that a command runs only where the user can watch and stop it.
findings.evidence: closewin.mjs drives the real createCommandWindowController with a fake window: attach() a live run, then win.close(). The handler at window.ts:177-185 only sets win = null, view = null and cancels announcements. Result: 'run stopped by closing the window? null' and no second window is made until something else needs one. createCommandWindow (windows.ts:54) has no 'close' interception. The only ways back are Settings (home/computers.ts:181 -> runtime.ts:855) or a bubble question's 'Show the command'.
findings.fix: While any tab is running (or a card/countdown is up), intercept the window's 'close' event: preventDefault and hide it, so tabs, Stop and output survive. If it must close, ask 'A command is still running. Stop it?' and call run.stop('user') on Yes. Add a 'Show' action to the task card and bubble while a command runs.

findings.title: Ask card: Allow and Not now fall below the fold for ordinary multi-line commands while a quarter of the window is empty
findings.scenario: The model asks to run a 10-line script (a heredoc that overwrites a config file, a multi-command deploy) with a couple of reasons. At the default 760x480 window the card area is capped at 72vh, so the card shows heading, a 192 px scrolling command, some reasons, then is cut off. Why:, the 'Read the whole command' hint, Allow and Not now are inside the outer scroller, under the fold, with about 120 px of empty black window below the cap. Two nested scrollbars appear, and a non-expert will think the card is broken or close it (see the close-window finding).
findings.evidence: cmd1.mjs screenshot shots/B-ask-ssh-long.png. probe-h.mjs for a 12-line command + 4 reasons: .cards bottom y=358, Allow top y=412 (cards scrollHeight 440 vs clientHeight 346), panels below it empty. sweep.mjs at 760x480 (X = Allow below the fold): 1 reason line + Why from 10 command lines; 2 reason lines from 9 lines; 4 reason lines from 6 lines. Long single lines wrap at about 90 characters, so a 550-character command is 6 lines.
findings.fix: Don't cap .cards when nothing sits below it (max-height: calc(100vh - 24px), or flex:1 when there are no tabs/pending lines). Better, make the action row sticky (position: sticky; bottom: 0 with the card's background) inside the card area, so Allow and Not now are always visible and only the command and reasons scroll.

findings.title: Copying command output: Ctrl+C interrupts a live run (Linux) or does nothing (Windows), no context menu, and the window can't be screenshotted on Windows/macOS
findings.scenario: A user selects an error message in the terminal and presses Ctrl+C. On a live Linux run, xterm sends ETX to the program (stopping it) and copies nothing. On an ended or Windows run nothing happens. There is no context menu or Copy button. Because the command window is content-protected on Windows and macOS (windows.ts:65), Snipping Tool or screen-share can't capture the output either, so to get an error out the user must retype it or know Ctrl+Insert.
findings.evidence: term-copy.mjs: select a row, Control+c -> clipboard '' and, for an interactive run, input '\u0003'; Control+Insert -> clipboard has the selected line; Control+Shift+c and Meta+c -> nothing. The docs never mention copying. macOS works through the Edit menu.
findings.fix: Custom key handler: Ctrl+C (Windows/Linux) with a selection copies and swallows the key, without a selection it is ^C; Ctrl+Shift+C always copies. Add a small 'Copy output' button next to Stop.

findings.title: Announcement card (countdown) omits the plain-language lines and the stop chord, and Stop is the quietest button
findings.scenario: The user said 'delete build/'. The command window shows 'Running this, as you asked', the raw rm -rf command, 'Starts in 4 s.' and a bordered grey Stop. The plain-language line ('Deletes build and everything in it.') and the model's Why: are in the card the window receives but buildAnnounce never draws them, so in 4 seconds the user must judge shell syntax. Nothing says the stop chord (Win+Alt+X / Ctrl+Alt+X) also works. The heading says 'Running' although nothing runs yet.
findings.evidence: shots/C-announce.png; buildAnnounce (main.ts:203-226) renders where, heading, command, legend, count, Stop only; card.says is unused there (it is built as [...d.says, why] in flow.ts:703). The bubble carries the plain sentence, but it is a separate window that can sit on another display.
findings.fix: Draw cardLines(card) under the command in the announcement, retitle it 'Starting in 4 s, as you asked', and add 'or press <stop chord>' under the countdown. Consider a 5-6 s countdown.

findings.title: Command card can be left with both buttons dead if the Confirmer refuses the answer
findings.scenario: Two tasks run; one is moving the mouse (borrow), or on macOS a key was just posted. The user clicks Allow on the command card, and Confirmer.answer() returns false while blocked(). The page has already set els.sent = true and disabled both buttons. Nothing re-enables them: re-showing the same card (the bubble's 'Show the command') keeps the same key, so the card stays frozen until the 2-minute expiry. The consent card has a recovery path for this (prompt-window.ts show()); the command card has none.
findings.evidence: stuck.mjs: after clicking Allow, allow.disabled and deny.disabled are true; after pushing the same card again (rev 2) both are still true. runtime.ts:915 confirmAnswer ignores the boolean from confirmer.answer; confirm.ts:152 returns false when blocked().
findings.fix: Have main push a state flag when an answer wasn't taken (or let the controller re-send the card with a new key/nonce), and let the page re-enable its buttons; or don't disable the buttons until the card actually leaves.

findings.title: Command and prompt windows aren't placed on Ember's display or visible on all workspaces
findings.scenario: With two monitors, Ember and the bubble ('May I run a command?', 'Needs you') are on the display the user is working on, but the always-on-top 760x480 command card, or the SSH password / consent window, opens with the default placement (the primary display's centre). On macOS the floating panel isn't on all Spaces or over a full-screen app. The user sees a bubble whose Allow lives in a window on another screen or Space; 'Show the command' makes it jump there.
findings.evidence: grep -rn 'setPosition|setBounds|center()|setVisibleOnAllWorkspaces' over commands/, remote/prompt-window.ts, windows.ts: nothing for these two windows; the overlay does use visibleOnFullScreen (platform/linux/overlay-shaper.ts:13). Electron's default is a centred position. Not reproducible in this single-display Linux container, so inferred from the code.
findings.fix: In reveal() (command) and prompt-window reveal(), place the window on the display nearest the cursor/Ember (screen.getDisplayNearestPoint) and call setVisibleOnAllWorkspaces(true, { visibleOnFullScreen: true, skipTransformProcessType: true }) while a card is up.

findings.title: After a remote helper's second check, a red 'refused it' tab for the same command lingers
findings.area: command window: tabs, remote second ask
findings.scenario: build-01's own gate finds more than the PC did, so the first run ends 'refused-remote' (needsConfirm) and the flow asks again with a new runId. The first tab stays: a red 'failed' symbol and 'build-01 refused it: build-01's own check wants the user's yes first: ...'. After the user says Allow a second tab for the same command runs. The user sees a failure for something they then approved, double-negative text included.
findings.evidence: flow.ts:749 assigns runId = newRunId() for the retry; window.ts:469 only drops a tab with the same runId ('a retry after the remote asked: its old tab goes'), so the comment's intent isn't met. command-flow.test.ts:1448 pins two different runIds. Code-read, not run live.
findings.fix: Have the flow tell the window to drop (or relabel 'Waiting for your OK again') the tab of a run that ended refused-remote with needsConfirm, or give the retry the same tab key.

findings.title: Card hierarchy: where a command runs and why are the quietest text; all asks look alike; leftover programs have no remedy
findings.area: command card: communication of place, reason, danger
findings.scenario: The computer a command will run on ('On build-01 as deploy') is 12 px at 66 % opacity above the heading, which says only 'Ember wants to run this command'. The model's Why: reason is 12 px at 52 %. A git push, a recursive delete, an 'ask every command' policy ask and a root ask all look the same, orange Allow included (the host-key card does demote its risky button, the command card doesn't), so with many cards users habituate. Ended tabs say '2 programs it started are still running: a, b.' with no Stop or hint how to end them, and a tab strip entry doesn't say which computer.
findings.evidence: shots/A-ask-local.png, B-ask-ssh-long.png, G-ended.png; styles.css:15 (.where) and :27 (.why); statusLine/stragglerText in copy.ts:82-110.
findings.fix: Put the computer in the heading for non-local targets ('...on build-01', with a small badge in the tab), give destructive classes a subtle marker (not a red alarm), and add a tip to the straggler line ('Ask Ember to stop them, or end them yourself').

findings.title: Stalled-link countdown re-announces every second to screen readers
findings.area: command window: accessibility of the status line
findings.scenario: When an SSH link goes quiet, remote-runner.ts:529 updates the status text every second ('This command stops in 14 s...' down to 0) and the page writes it into a role='status' (polite live) element, so a screen reader reads about 17 near-identical announcements over the grace period.
findings.evidence: main.ts:267 sets role='status' on each tab's status line; remote-runner.ts:521-531 steps the countdown each second; window.ts note() pushes state per change.
findings.fix: Keep the visible countdown but move it out of the live region (aria-live='off' on the countdown), announce once when the link stalls and once when it resumes or the command stops.

findings.title: Command block is a focusable <pre> with aria-label, so a screen reader gets a label for the command instead of the command
findings.area: Command window: names and roles (ARIA 1.2 naming prohibited on generic)
findings.scenario: A screen-reader user Tabs to the card's command block (it has tabIndex=0 so it can be scrolled). It is exposed as a generic with the name 'The command, every character shown', and many readers speak the name and not the text. The safety-critical content (the command, with zero-width and mixed-script characters made visible) is only reached by browse-mode reading. Tabbing to Allow gives no description of the command either.
findings.evidence: CDP tree (command.mjs): `generic name="The command, every character shown" focusable=true` with the command only as a child StaticText. axe reports aria-prohibited-attr (needs review) on this node, for both the card and the tab panel's block. The ask card in the same window labels its region from the heading, which works.
findings.fix: Use role='textbox' aria-readonly='true' aria-multiline='true' with the aria-label (the command is then its value), or role='group' with aria-labelledby pointing at the heading and the command itself as content; remove the aria-label from the bare <pre>. Give Allow aria-describedby pointing at the command block.

findings.title: Command approval card shows a tool name and model-directed advice: "Open apps with open_app instead."
findings.scenario: The user's task runs `gedit notes.txt`, `firefox …`, `notepad` or `regedit`. The Allow / Not now card reads "Ember can't tell exactly what this does.", then "Open apps with open_app instead.", then "You didn't ask for this." open_app is an internal tool name and the sentence is advice to the model, so it is meaningless to the person deciding. The same card also carries phrasing like "Ember can't tell what ls is given.", "It uses $ExecutionContext.", "It uses a translated string." and "It spells the program with ^ escapes."
findings.evidence: Ran classifyCommand and decideCommand from the test fixtures: `gedit notes.txt` gives says = ["Ember can't tell exactly what this does.","Open apps with open_app instead.","You didn't ask for this."], and the same for firefox, notepad, regedit and Out-GridView. `ls $(pwd)` gives "Ember can't tell what ls is given." `echo $"hi"` gives "It uses a translated string." SAYS.openApp is used at classify.ts:1922, 3336, 4410, 4703, 4845 and 5101, and `says` goes straight to the card (flow.ts:671-676).
findings.fix: Reword for the reader: "This opens an app window, which Ember can do itself without a command. Say no and ask Ember to open it." Also: "Ember can't tell which arguments ls gets.", "It uses PowerShell's $ExecutionContext, which Ember can't follow.", "It uses locale-translated text ($\"…\"), which Ember can't check."

findings.title: The approval question names controls with accessibility jargon: "Click “Save” push button in Mousepad?"
findings.scenario: The question seen most often in the product uses the raw AT-SPI role: "Click “Save” push button in Mousepad?", "Switch “Night Light” toggle button in Settings?", "Choose “Vegetarian” in “Meal” combo box…", "Click “Advanced” page tab…". The same Settings page's activity list uses friendly words ("a button", "a drop-down", "a tab"), so the vocabulary is inconsistent. Windows and macOS use the same names because roles.ts maps them to the AT-SPI vocabulary.
findings.evidence: Probe of plainQuestion (probe2) printed exactly those four strings plus "Borrow your mouse to click “Send” push button in Mousepad?". app/sidecar-host/roles.ts:6 states buttons are "push button" on every OS.
findings.fix: Map roles for the question the way home/copy.ts ROLE does: push button → button, toggle button → switch, combo box → drop-down, page tab → tab, check box → checkbox, radio button → option, e.g. "Click the “Save” button in Mousepad?" Share one table between the question and the activity list.

findings.title: The command card mixes "I" and "Ember"
findings.scenario: The command window card is written in the third person ("Ember wants to run this command", "Ember can't tell exactly what this does.", "You asked Ember to check every command with you."), but two lines switch to first person: "I'm checking each step: a step came up that you didn't ask for." and "I'm checking each step: an earlier command printed text that looked like instructions." The bubbles are first person by design; the card is not.
findings.evidence: decide.ts:26, flow.ts:111 and 210. target-copy.ts's header says first person is for bubbles.
findings.fix: "Ember is checking each step: a step came up that you didn't ask for." (and likewise for the output line). Update the pinned strings.

findings.title: Mixed-script marker underlines the user's own folders (even ASCII words) on every card and tab for non-Latin usernames and folders, with no legend on tabs
findings.area: command window: mixed-script marking, alarm fatigue
findings.platforms: windows, linux, macos (users with non-Latin folder names)
findings.scenario: A Russian, Greek, Arabic or Japanese user has C:\Users\Иван or ~/Документы. The main script is judged per whitespace token, and paths are one token, so the Cyrillic name in C:\Users\Иван flips the verdict and 'C:' and 'Users' are underlined yellow; in /home/ana/Документы/проект the ASCII 'home' and 'ana' are. Every card for this user shows the underlined header (the default cwd is the home folder) plus the legend 'Letters from another alphabet are underlined.'; every tab, even for a harmless Get-ChildItem that never asked, shows the same underlines with no legend at all. The one signal meant to catch a look-alike letter (buіld) becomes noise for this population.
findings.evidence: vt.mjs: visibleText marks 'C:\Users\[Иван]', '/[home]/[ana]/Документы', 'cp ~/Загрузки/[file].[txt]', 'cd C:\Users\[Ανδρέας]\Desktop'. Renders shots/L-cyrillic-user.png and shots/V-tab-cyrillic.png. In buildTab (main.ts:259, 278) the legend returned by commandBlock/headerNode is discarded; document .legend count on the tab is 0. visible-text.test.ts only pins single filenames (日本語.txt), not paths.
findings.fix: Judge the main script per word, not per whitespace token: split at path and punctuation characters (/ \ . - _ : ~ = ,) before counting scripts, so Иван, Users and project are each single-script while buіld, рm and gіt are still flagged. Show the legend on tabs too or don't mark in tabs. Consider a plain sentence line ('Some letters look like another alphabet') only for true intra-word mixing.

findings.title: RTL text reorders on the command card: what is shown is not the order that runs
findings.scenario: The card's promise is that what you approve is what runs, and it makes explicit bidi controls visible. Plain Hebrew or Arabic letters need no control characters to be reordered by the Unicode bidi algorithm: digits and neutrals next to an RTL word swap places. The tokens aren't flagged because the characters are ordinary. For Hebrew or Arabic users (or a crafted command) the displayed argument order can differ from the real one; the terminal below shows logical order, so card and terminal disagree.
findings.evidence: bidi.mjs: logical 'chmod -R 755 שלום 777 /srv/data'; rendered left to right 'chmod -R 755 777 שלום /srv/data' (shots/W-rtl.png). .command sets no direction or unicode-bidi.
findings.fix: On .command and the header: direction: ltr; unicode-bidi: bidi-override (or wrap RTL runs in <bdo dir=ltr>), so the card shows logical order like the shell and xterm; note it in the legend.
